text: After much deliberation, we are still unable to come to a unanimous decision. In order to bring 12 minds to a unanimous result, you must examine the questions submitted to you with candor and with proper regard and deference and respect to the opinions of each other. The Lindsay Clancy trial may now end without a verdict at all. After five days and almost 30 hours of deliberations, the jury has told the judge twice that they cannot unanimously agree on what should happen to her. And we are now getting very close to a possible mistrial. Quick reminder, Lindsay Clancy killed all three of her children in January 2023. That part isn't disputed. The question is whether she was criminally responsible. Her defense says Lindsay was suffering from postpartum psychosis and was so detached from reality that she should be found not criminally responsible. The prosecution says she was severely depressed but not psychotic, understood what she was doing and should be convicted. And just as an interesting side note, one of the prosecution's main psychiatric experts, Dr. Avram Mak, resigned from his hospital job on the same day he finished testifying. The hospital says he resigned, not that he was fired, and they have not said why. So, I'm not saying the two things are connected, but the timing is definitely interesting. After more than five weeks of trial, over 80 witnesses and around 300 exhibits, the case finally went to the jury. And another interesting detail, the 12 jurors actually deciding the case are 9 women and 3 men. Again, I'm not suggesting that means anything by itself, but considering how overwhelmingly female the public support for Lindsay has been, it is at least something I found interesting. The jury started deliberating on August 27th and they apparently cannot agree. On Tuesday, they told Judge William Sullivan for the first time that they couldn't reach a unanimous decision. He told them to keep deliberating. Then on Wednesday, they came back and told him essentially the same thing again. They were still deadlocked. This time, the judge gave them something called a Tui-Rodriguez instruction, sometimes referred to as a dynamite charge. Despite the dramatic name, it basically means go back, listen carefully to the other jurors, reconsider your position, and make every reasonable effort to reach an agreement. But don't abandon an honest belief just because everyone else disagrees with you. This is generally one of the last steps a judge can take with a deadlocked jury. And even after receiving that instruction, they still finished the day without a verdict. So what happens if they simply cannot agree? The judge can eventually declare a mistrial. And importantly, a mistrial does not mean Lindsay is acquitted. It means this particular jury couldn't reach a verdict. The prosecution could then decide to put Lindsay on trial again with an entirely new jury. And Lindsay also wouldn't just automatically walk out of the hospital where she's currently being held. At the time I'm recording this, however, there is still no mistrial and still no verdict. And considering they have now twice told the judge that they cannot agree, whatever happens next is going to be very interesting.
